We strongly condemn this attack and extend our deepest condolences to the bereaved families of the fallen peacekeepers. We wish the injured a swift recovery. This tragedy underscores why the safety and security of peacekeepers must remain a collective priority. As co-sponsor of Security Council Resolution 2823, Kyrgyzstan reiterates the need for the prompt identification and prosecutions of perpetrators, as well as thorough investigations into attacks against peacekeepers. Looking ahead, We see the need for renewed focus on peacemaking and preventive diplomacy, stronger partnerships with host states, focus and adaptable mandates, early transition planning, greater operational readiness and accountability, and closer regional cooperation. This work must remain member state-led. Any adaptation must preserve consent, impartiality, and the non-use of force except in self-defense and defense of the mandate. Institutional reform and technology cannot substitute for political will. As a contributor of military and police personnel, Kyrgyzstan will continue to support effective and accountable United Nations peace operations. This success should ultimately be measured by whether the advanced political settlements protect civilians and contribute to sustainable nationality on peace. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kyrgyzstan, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Fiji, followed by Angola, then Ukraine.

Thank you, Madam President. At the outset, I would like to pay tribute to the fallen peacekeepers of Ethiopia. The Government of the Republic of Fiji thanks the President and the General Assembly for the opportunity to provide comments on the Secretary-General's report on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations. Fiji welcomes this timely and important report, which comes at a moment when conflicts are becoming more complex, contracted, and difficult to resolve. and when the need for the effective, principled and well-resourced peace operations remains as urgent as ever. Fiji aligns itself with the message of the report. Peace operations must remain anchored in political solutions, the consent and cooperation of host states, impartiality and respect for international law. We also agree that mandates must be clear, focused, adaptable and matched by realistic resources and capabilities. In increasingly dangerous operating environments, peacekeepers must be equipped with the tools, training and technology necessary to protect themselves, support mandate implementation and contribute meaningfully to the protection of civilians. For Fiji, peacekeeping is not only a contribution to international peace and security, it is a longstanding national commitment. For decades, Fijian military and police personnel have served with dedication, courage, and humility in United Nations missions around the world. Our experience has reinforced the importance of strong partnerships among the Security Council, the Secretariat, host states, troops and political contributing countries, regional organizations, and affected communities. Fiji therefore supports efforts to strengthen the effectiveness, agility, and accountability of peace operations, including through improved readiness, better situational awareness, responsible use of new technologies. Fiji also welcomes the report's emphasis on strengthen partnerships with regional organizations, and support for regional peace efforts. In conclusion, Fiji reaffirms its steadfast commitment to United Nations peacekeeping and to the collective effort to make peace operations more effective, credible, and fit for purpose. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Fiji and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Angola.

Madam President, thank you for giving me the floor. Angola thanks the President of the General Assembly for convening this meeting and the Secretary-General for presenting its reports on the future of United Nations peace operations prepared pursuant to Action 21 of the Pact for the Future. Angola recognizes that the current international environment marked by geopolitical fragmentation, the proliferation of conflicts, and erosion of respect for international law, requires peace operations that are more agile, flexible, effective, and responsive to realities on the ground. However, technical and institutional reforms, while essential, cannot substitute the political will required to address this challenging reality. The success of peace operations depends on clear and realistic mandates, adequate Predictable and sustainable financing is also essential. The safety and security of peacekeepers must remain our top priority. Peace operation must support and never replace nationally led political processes. Effective cooperation is another key component to build sustainable peace, including cooperation among Security Council, the secretariats, and troop and police contributing countries. Angola underscores the importance of the principle of peaceful settlement of disputes, conflict prevention, peace building, and national ownership. As part of its regional effort to contribute to preventive diplomacy, the African Union Extraordinary Summit on Strengthening Mechanisms for Conflict Prevention and Resolution in Africa is taking place in Angola on 29th and 30th of August. In this context, We reiterate the need for further strengthening the strategic partnership between the United Nations and the African Union in accordance with chapter seven of the charter of United Nations and Security Council Resolution 2719, including through appropriate financing arrangement for African Union-led peace support operation authorized by Security Council. Angola stands ready to engage constructively in the discussion of the recommendation and finding contained in the Secretary-General's reports, and would like to ask for further information on the next steps. The reform process should result in a peace operation system that is more coherent, accountable, and capable of protecting population, supporting durable political processes, and responding effectively to the needs and conflicts affect the countries. Angola, in conclusion, presents its deepest condolences to Somalia for the loss of the two peacekeepers in line of duty and wish quick recovery for those injured. Thank you, Madam President.

I thank the distinguished representative of Angola, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ukraine, who will be followed by the observer for the African Union and the observer for the International Organization of La Francophonie.

Madam Vice President, let me begin by thanking President Annalena Baerbock for convening this crucial discussion and Secretary General Antonio Guterres for presenting this comprehensive review. As you know, Ukraine has been one of the biggest contributors to the UN peacekeeping operations during the last decades. The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine in 2014, as well as the full-scale military invasion in 2022, have made it impossible, unfortunately. Our soldiers must now defend our homeland. But as a country that continues to defend itself against this aggression, Ukraine does appreciate the importance of effective UN tools and conflict prevention, conflict management, and the maintenance of international peace and security. In this regard, we welcome the Secretary-General's efforts to ensure that UN peacekeeping operations remain fit for purpose in a rapidly changing security environment. As we are discussing the future of UN peace operations, we should not forget that one of the Secretary-General's

previous reports on this very subject established a very clear safeguard

for their integrity. Those states parties repeatedly listed for grave violations against children or conflict-related sexual violence should not be accepted for participation in UN peacekeeping operations. That policy was subsequently endorsed by the UN Security Council. Today, the credibility of that policy is being tested Let me remind the Assembly that Russian armed forces have been blacklisted for grave violations against children for four consecutive years. Let me repeat, four consecutive years. Moreover, this year the Russian army was also blacklisted for patterns of conflict-related sexual violence. Yet, Russian personnel continue to serve under the UN flag. We cannot seriously debate how to make peacekeeping stronger while disregarding safeguards designed to protect its integrity. A blue helmet cannot become a privilege enjoyed irrespective of the conduct of the forces behind it. We therefore call upon the UN Secretary-General to take all necessary steps regarding Russia's continued participation in UN peacekeeping operations. There shall be no impunity. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ukraine, and I give the floor to the distinguished observer of the African Union.

Madam President, I thank the PGA for convening this meeting and the Secretary-General for his report and briefing. I welcome the presence of the Chief of Staff and USGs. Most of the UN peacekeepers serve in Africa and most of the operations under review touch our continent. We express condolences to Ethiopia and to pay tribute to all peacekeepers. I would like to make few remarks from the perspective of the African Union Commission. The AU Commission welcomes the report's treatment of the global regional partnership The Secretary-General is right that resolution 2719 was more than a financial instrument. It renewed the interpretation of chapter eight of the charter and the commitment of member states to share responsibility for international peace and security. We particularly welcome the recommendation that the Security Council act proactively, case by case, in authorizing support for African Union-led peace support operations. The task now is implementation, The joint AU UN roadmap in this regard is advancing. Where mandated operations are in transition, the report's own warning applies with particular force. The abrupt or premature withdrawal of support risks undoing hard-won gains. Orderly and predictable successor arrangements must be found. We welcome the report's insistence on the primacy of politics and that peacekeeping as a core work of this organization. This week, our AU assembly convenes an extraordinary session in Luanda, Angola, devoted to strengthening the continent's mechanism for conflict prevention and resolution. As well, the wider United Nations system must carry pragmatic, programmatic delivery and predictable resources for peacebuilding. Peacebuilding is not only the path out of missions invested early in prevention, it reduces the need for them as member states recognized by consensus in the 2025 PBAR review. Mandates must be matched with resources. The African Union carries its share, including capitalization of peace of the peace fund. Finally, we welcome the Secretary-General's statement that adapting peace operations to a changed world requires a more representative Security Council addressing the historical injustice of Africa. The African Union stands ready to work with all member states as this report moves into intergovernmental consideration with the women, peace and security and youth, peace and security agendas integrated all through. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished observer of the African Union, and I now give the floor to the distinguished observer of the International Organization of La Francophonie.

Madam President, we would like to thank the Secretary-General for presenting his report, and we express our thanks for the quality of the consultation held as the report was being drafted. The Francophonie is fully committed to these consultations in order to reaffirm our attachment to the effectiveness of peacekeeping operations, the strengthening of French speakers in these missions and strengthening French in these missions when the context so requires, in the interests of respecting various cultures. We very much appreciate that the report several times echoes the Rabat Declaration adopted last May during the second ministerial conference on the maintenance of peace in French-speaking countries and the primacy of political solutions and the importance of clear and realistic mandates and the the strengthening of developing strategic operational partnerships. All of those things are essential pillars of the French vision for peacekeeping operations. We very much appreciate the deepening partnerships with regional organizations and non-UN organizations as well. That should enable us to take advantage of the comparative advantage of each of these players with a clear distribution of roles as well as mechanisms that are adapted in terms of coordination and mobility. In this regard, we would call for a full implementation and operationalisation of Resolution 2719 of the Security Council. The International Organisation of Francophonie also welcomes the attention that has been paid to the transition and continuity of peace building after the withdrawal of a peacekeeping operation. The modalities for this continuity should be explained further, particularly as they relate to regional organisations and international organisations in the area of prevention, mediation and governance, the rule of law and national capacity building. The OIF would also like to stress another important thing multilingualism must be recognised as a general operational capacity, speaking the language used in the country of deployment. and having intercultural skills helps to improve knowledge of the area and helps relations with the population and coordination within the mission and more broadly helps promote ownership of the peace process. Finally, we would encourage a more structured relationship with regard to when missions are being conceived and implemented with the local population. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished observer of the International Organization of La Francophonie. We have heard the last speaker for this meeting. And so I now give the floor to the Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations, Mr. Jean-Pierre Lecoart, and the Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, Ms. Rosemary DiCarlo.

Madam President, I would like to thank all Member States for their statements, which I won't attempt to summarise. There were a lot of important things that have been said in the review and that were mentioned by various speakers today. There were questions, however, about follow up. for this study and on that I'd just like to make a couple of comments and the first and I think this is the most fundamental is that just as the process that led to the preparation of the review was a collaborative and inclusive process and I'd like to thank the very many Member States that referred to that part of the process Equally, our intention is to have the same approach when it comes to follow-up of the review because nothing can be done without our Member States, the troop contributing countries, the police contributing countries, the members of the Security Council, the C-34 members, and also our financial contributors. Some speakers referred to the C-34 and I can tell you that's something, the sentiment that I also share. The C-34 plays a very important role in its capacity as the organ which adopts guidelines on the most important matters relating to peacekeeping and I believe that the C-34 should play an important role as well in the follow-up and implementation of this review and of course it will be up to member states to determine exactly how this should be done in practice. Of course, a number of recommendations in the review pointed to the practices of certain organs such as the Security Council for example and the issue related to the mandate and to the priorities that are contained in those mandates. This is a question of Security Council practice. I would also stress here the importance of unified political support of the Security Council that was stressed in the report, not just for the operations themselves but also for the political process through which these missions are created. This is fundamental. It is also a practical issue for Member States and the Security Council. To be more specific now, a number of recommendations contained in the review are linked to work that is already underway under action for peacekeeping and action for peacekeeping impact and also in other initiatives, for example, the digital transformation in peacekeeping and also the security of peacekeepers and the work that we have been doing on drones and the threat that they represent. But again, this is work that is being done and cannot be done without close cooperation with Member States. And of course, that is what guarantees their success. Now, a number of new processes will are going to begin some have already begun a couple of examples the review mentions in paragraph 62a the launching of a study on key capacities for the military and police that are necessary for operations this review is going to begin shortly. We're already in the process of pulling together the team that will lead this. And once again, this is something that will be very collaborative and inclusive with member states because, of course, it's member states that provide us with the capacity that we're talking about. In the same paragraph, 62a, of the report, it mentions the importance of strengthening flexibility in force generation and force capacity and staff capacity, increasing the number and category of contributors. And this is work that we have begun, of course, with the Support Office, Department for Peacekeeping Support. Those are a couple of things that I wanted to say with regard to the implementation of this review and you can count on the Department of Peace Operations to address this new phase in a very cooperative and inclusive spirit with our Member States. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Excellencies, thank you so much for your comments today. Thanks to many of you who made contributions to the report. We carried out quite an extensive consultation process before the drafting, and we intend to continue these consultations. I do want to thank you also for your citizens, our UN colleagues who work in SPMs and PKOs. many of whom risked their lives in the cause of peace, and my condolences to the government and people of Ethiopia for their recent loss. But without them, we could not do this work. Going forward, yes, we will continue our consultations. We will be consulting with member states, with regional organizations, civil society on the recommendations, as we did before we started the drafting. We will also find opportunities to follow up with you. We'll send you information about ways that we can meet and talk further about the recommendations going forward. It's very important that we work together. After all, it is your organization and it is all of our colleagues and your citizens who are trying to carry this forward. So thank you again and we will be in touch shortly.

I thank the Secretary-General, Chief of Cabinet, USG's and their team for their participation in this meeting today. I thank all delegations for their participation. This informal meeting of the plenary is now concluded. The meeting is now adjourned.
